_comment: THE CONTRACT BETWEEN FOUR IMPLEMENTATIONS OF ONE RULE.
Which metrics does a schema model? Four places answer it, in three languages, because they run
in four processes that cannot import one another:
frontend/src/utils/deviceTags.js          modelledMetrics()    -- the browser
ingestion/validate.py                     modelled_metrics()   -- the conformance validator
i3x/i3x_service.py                        _modelled_metrics()  -- the i3X address space
supabase/functions/aas-export/index.ts    modelledMetrics()    -- the AAS exporter
This file is the seam. Each asserts every case below in its own runner, in the CI job that
already runs it -- vitest, two unittest suites, and (for the Deno one) a Node harness in
test_aas_export.py that executes the function rather than grepping it.
WHY A FIXTURE RATHER THAN A grep. The rule is behaviour, not a literal. A grep asserting that
both files mention `required` proves they both spell it, not that they agree about a schema
whose `required` is a string. Writing this file found a divergence that had been shipping:
for `properties: ['A','B']` the JS returned {'0','1'} -- the ARRAY INDICES as metric names,
because `typeof [] === 'object'` and `Object.keys` on an array yields its indices -- while the
Python returned null. A device with such a schema was judged against metrics called '0' and
'1' in the dashboard, so almost everything it published read as Unmodelled, while validate.py
reported it had no model at all.
AND IT FOUND THE SAME ONE AGAIN, LATER, IN A COPY THAT HAD NEVER BEEN ADDED HERE. The
aas-export implementation was written from the uncorrected JS and inherited the array bug,
then sat outside the contract while this comment described the bug it was carrying. It was
the worst place for it: those names become Submodel Property idShorts in an exported AAS
shell -- a document handed to a third party, asserting metrics no device ever published -- and
'0' cannot begin an AAS idShort, so the shell fails validation at the CONSUMER while the
exporter reports success. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS FILE ALREADY TAUGHT: a fifth
implementation that is not listed above is a fifth implementation that is not checked.
THE EXPECTED VALUES BELOW ARE THE PYTHON SEMANTICS, because they are the correct ones: an
array is not a valid JSON Schema `properties` object, and inventing metric names from its
indices is meaningless. Every other implementation was corrected to match.
`expected: null` means the schema declares neither and therefore CANNOT BE EVALUATED -- which
is different from modelling nothing, and is why Unmodelled is not reported for a device with
no usable schema. Do not collapse null and [] IN THE MIRRORS THAT DISTINGUISH THEM.
TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS DELIBERATELY DO COLLAPSE THEM, and that is not drift. i3X and the AAS
exporter both iterate the result to decide what to project or emit; neither has a caller that
asks 'was this evaluable?', and neither format can express the answer. Their suites compare
the NAMES against `expected or []` and assert the collapse explicitly, so it stays a stated
property rather than an accident. The names themselves must agree exactly in all four.
Adding a case here is the way to extend the contract: all four suites read every case.

cases.name: both, overlapping — the union, not a duplicate
empty definition — declares neither, so not evaluable
explicitly empty properties and required — still not evaluable
required is a string, not a list — ignored, properties still count
properties is an ARRAY — malformed, contributes nothing (was the divergence)
properties is an array AND required is valid — only required counts
properties is a string — malformed, contributes nothing
